title: What causes Motion Sickness & How To Stop It?
tags: how to stop motion sickness on rides
description:
Ever felt dizzy, nauseous, or sweaty while traveling in a car, plane, or boat? Or maybe during an amusement park ride, or even watching a shaky film like The Blair Witch Project? That unpleasant feeling is called motion sickness, and it affects about 1 in 3 people worldwide. From kids on school trips to astronauts in rockets, no one is entirely immune. But what exactly causes this strange phenomenon?

In this episode of Pale Blue Thoughts, we explore the science behind motion sickness. It happens when your senses send conflicting signals to the brain. Your eyes, ears, and body all report different information — and your brain, unable to reconcile them, reacts with dizziness, nausea, and even vomiting. The key player is the vestibular system in the inner ear, with semicircular canals and fluid-filled sacs that help balance and orientation. When the eyes see stillness but the ear senses motion, the brain interprets it as a possible hallucination or even poisoning, triggering the vomit reflex

Motion Sickness

.

Scientists have proposed multiple hypotheses: neurotransmitters activating the “vomit center” in the brain, evolutionary defenses against toxins, and even stimulation of the vagus nerve. Women, children, and pregnant people tend to be more susceptible. Motion sickness can be triggered by cars, ships, planes, rollercoasters, VR headsets, and even IMAX screens. While ginger, lemons, and chewing gum are often touted as cures, the most effective remedies involve reducing sensory mismatch — like looking at the horizon, choosing a front seat, or reclining to minimize conflicting signals.

If you’ve searched for motion sickness explained, why people vomit while traveling, how to prevent seasickness, science of nausea, vestibular system balance, motion sickness remedies, this video gives you the rational perspective.
